opening_message:
Ticket 1: Terri Koch (employee ID E009) requests admin access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E009.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Engineer
  - employment type: full_time
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Terri Koch (E009), full-time Engineer, requests admin to Payroll. Full-time employees may have up to write; admin requires the employee's role to own the system, and Engineer does not own Payroll. Recommend granting write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Engineer
  - employment type: contractor
  - security training: basic
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E009 (Terri Koch) is a contractor with basic security training. Contractors max is read (write only with advanced training, never admin). Requested admin exceeds maximum, so recommend granting read.
reason: Terri Koch (E009) requests admin access to Payroll. Admin is above the maximum under either set of facts: if full-time Engineer, max is write (Engineer does not own Payroll); if contractor with basic security training (per Security DB note), max is read and never admin. Because the facts conflict and admin is never permitted, I grant the more conservative maximum, which is read.

- Note 2 (from ticket 1): role Engineer, employment type contractor, security training basic, recommendation read

2. contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin. If contractor with basic training, max is read. Requested admin > read, so grant read.

So HR says full-time, Security says contractor with basic training.

In many such scenarios, the Security DB note should be authoritative for such facts. So contractor + basic training → max read. Requested admin > read → grant read.
